newsitem.title: USA: Carolina Power has major damage after Fran.
newsitem.headline: Carolina Power has major damage after Fran.

text.p: Hurricane Fran, which roared through North Carolina late Thursday, has left 670,000 of Carolina Power & Light Co's customers without electricity and caused heavy damage to the utility's transmission lines, the company said Friday.
"This was a direct hit on our service area," said company spokesman Mike Hughes.
"We have 670,000 customers without power out of a customer base of 1.1 million. That's nearly two-thirds of our customers, the vast majority of them in North Carolina."

Hughes said this was about three times as many as were left without power after Hurricane Bertha, which brushed along the Carolina coast in July, causing an estimated $8 million to $10 million in damage to Carolina Power's system.
"We also have some significant damage to our transmission lines, which is going to prolong recovery efforts," he said.

Hughes said initial reports estimate about 40 of the utility's transmission lines - the main lines carrying power from generating plants to local distribution lines - were either downed or damaged by the storm.
He said there was also extensive damage to large distribution lines, adding "I wouldn't even try to guess at the number of smaller distribution lines that are down."

Much of the damage is on what he called "the other side of the meter", referring to homes and businesses which, because of structural damage, could not receive power even if it were available to them.
"One of our main problems is getting crews out there to survey the damage. There are trees and debris all over, blocking the roads."
He said the 1,521 megawatt Brunswick nuclear power facility, shut early Thursday as a precaution ahead of the storm, had pulled through with damage only to an administrative and maintenance building.
The plant's two reactors were unscathed.
The Brunswick, at Southport, N.C., lies just west of Cape Fear on the state's southernmost coast, where Fran came smashing ashore with winds of up to 120 mph (193 kph).
Fran was downgraded early Friday to a tropical storm as it continues to move inland.
Hughes said it was still raining in Raleigh, N.C., where the company is headquartered, and that there was some local flooding.
"There are widepread outages this far inland as well. At this time we have no estimates for how long it's going to take to get power back to everyone. It was a very powerful storm."
-- J Jelter, New York Power Desk +1 212 859 1621
